chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hassan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Saif ibn 'Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a person in ihram who was compelled to eat game or meat of an animal that died naturally. He said: 'Which is more preferable to you, to eat from the game or the meat of an animal that died naturally?' I said: 'The meat of an animal that died naturally, because the game is forbidden to the person in ihram.' He said: 'Which is more preferable to you, to eat from your own wealth or the meat of an animal that died naturally?' I said: 'I eat from my own wealth.' He said: 'Then eat from the game and redeem it.'

key_terms.الصَّيْدُ: Game (wild animals permissible to eat generally but forbidden during ihram)
key_terms.الْمَيْتَةُ: Meat of an animal that died naturally (permanently forbidden)
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: A person in the state of ihram (ritual consecration) for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.وَفَاءُ الصَّيْدِ: Redemption of the game (paying a penalty in kind or value for eating game during ihram)

ai.seo_question: What should a pilgrim in ihram eat if forced to choose between game and dead meat?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *al-Istibsar*, illustrating the Shia juristic principle of *ikhtiyar al-adnab* (choosing the lesser of two evils) through the Imam’s dialectical questioning. By comparing the temporary prohibition of game during *ihram* against the permanent prohibition of carrion, the Imam establishes that the pilgrim should consume the game and pay the *fidya* (redemption penalty), thereby preserving the sanctity of the permanent dietary laws while managing the specific ritual restriction.
